name: Blankenhorn v. City of Orange
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California, District Judge Gary L. Taylor)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, three officers gang tackled a misdemeanor trespass suspect who refused to kneel without first trying to handcuff him, punches to a prone arrestee, hobble restraints on wrists and ankles after handcuffing, probable cause to arrest, failure to train evidence limited to one officer, supervisory liability for approving evaluations despite excessive force complaints
summary: Orange police stopped a man who had been banned from a shopping mall six months earlier, and when he refused an order to kneel to be handcuffed, three officers tackled him at once without first trying to handcuff him, one punched him in the head and body, and he was placed in hobble restraints on his wrists and ankles after he was cuffed. The Ninth Circuit held the officers had probable cause for the trespass arrest but reversed summary judgment on the excessive force claims for the gang tackle, the punches and the hobble restraints, holding that Graham's rule that force is justified only by a need for force gave clear notice. It affirmed summary judgment for the city because the failure to train evidence concerned a single officer, but reinstated the claim against the chief who approved that officer's evaluations despite prior excessive force complaints. It is the Ninth Circuit's basic takedown case.
coverage: The opinion by Judge King (sitting by designation), Judge Berzon's partial concurrence and dissent, and all footnotes were read in full from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/485/485.F3d.463.04-55938.html. The archive heads the file 485 F.3d 463, No. 04-55938, argued and submitted March 6, 2006, filed May 8, 2007, which confirms the citation.

The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The Ninth Circuit's slip opinion was not available at the court's archive for the 2007 filing date.
The mall security video is described only as the court described it; the court noted that a pole obstructs much of the view and that the video has no audio.
No subsequent history (remand proceedings or trial result) was checked.
facts:
The court viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to Blankenhorn, the party opposing summary judgment, and relied on a mall security video with no audio and an obstructed view.

On February 4, 2001, security at The Block at Orange, a shopping mall, issued Gary Blankenhorn a written notice forbidding him from returning. Sergeant Gray knew he had been banned. In early July 2001, Officer Ross interviewed Blankenhorn near a reported gang fight at the mall and found him completely calm and cooperative. About midnight on July 28, 2001, Gray saw Blankenhorn in a crowd at the mall and asked Officer Nguyen to help find him so they could identify him and ask whether security wanted him removed. Nguyen's report described him as a known 18th Street gang member who had been banned. They found him talking with an adult friend, the friend's younger brother and another boy.

The accounts of the stop differ. On Blankenhorn's version, Nguyen yelled at him from fifteen feet to come over, would not say why, and when Blankenhorn tried to walk away blocked him and grabbed his arm. Blankenhorn yanked free, and Nguyen threatened to spray him with mace. Blankenhorn admits he was angry, loud and profane and that he threw his driver's license on the ground. The officers reported a fighting stance and clenched fists and said he announced his gang membership; Blankenhorn and his friend denied this, and the video shows gestures and pointing but no clenched fists. Detective South arrived as backup and a mall guard joined them.

Nguyen asked Blankenhorn to kneel so he could be handcuffed. Blankenhorn refused, saying he was not going to his knees. On his account, Nguyen, Ross and South immediately jumped on him together; the officers say Nguyen first reached for his wrist. The video shows several seconds of struggle before the three took him to the ground. He was handcuffed, and Gray ordered Ross to apply ripp hobble restraints to his wrists and ankles. The video clearly shows Nguyen punch Blankenhorn in the head and twice in the side, at least once after he was on the ground; Blankenhorn says an officer also pressed a knee into the back of his neck. The officers' reports did not mention the punches but said he resisted handcuffing by pulling his hands under his body, which he denies and the video does not resolve. Officer Kayano arrived during the struggle and held his left arm for handcuffing.

Blankenhorn was charged with trespass, three counts of resisting arrest and disturbing the peace, with a gang enhancement. At the preliminary hearing Nguyen admitted the punches, and the prosecutor dismissed everything, concerned about his credibility. By then Blankenhorn had spent three months in jail.

He sued under section 1983 for unlawful arrest, excessive force and malicious prosecution, sued the city and Chief Romero for municipal and supervisory liability, and brought state tort claims. The district court granted summary judgment to all defendants on everything.
holding:
Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.

Arrest. The officers had probable cause to arrest for trespass given the prior written ban and security's request, and in any event the trespass statutes were unclear enough that qualified immunity applied. Judge Berzon disagreed on probable cause but concurred on immunity.

Excessive force: the gang tackle. The court stressed that a lawful arrest does not settle the force question. A rational jury could find the tackle by Nguyen, Ross and South unreasonable. The crime, misdemeanor trespass, was minimal. A jury could conclude from Blankenhorn's cooperation with Ross three weeks earlier, his casual conversation when found, and the officers' own relaxed conduct on the video (Nguyen standing with arms folded, patrons allowed within feet) that he posed no serious threat. The pace of events did not call for the latitude Graham gives split second judgments. And although he verbally refused to kneel, a jury could find that Nguyen never tried to handcuff him and that he was not actively resisting when the three officers tackled him.

Hobble restraints. The court accepted that hobbles may be reasonable to control a person who physically struggled during arrest. But a person has a limited right to offer reasonable resistance to an arrest that is the product of an officer's bad faith or provocative conduct (United States v. Span, Arpin). An officer who uses excessive force is not acting in good faith, so the jury question on the tackle precluded a finding of good faith as a matter of law. The court also held the officers' conduct could reasonably be considered provocative: no warning that an arrest was coming, no attempt to handcuff, and three officers simultaneously wrestling him down as if on a predetermined signal. The video appears to show Blankenhorn trying to stay on his feet without striking anyone, so a jury could find his resistance reasonable, which would make the later hobble restraints unreasonable.

Punches. Nguyen testified he punched to free Blankenhorn's arms from under his body, a distraction technique. Blankenhorn denies pinning his arms and the video is unclear. If he did not, there was no need for force to free them, and the need for force is at the heart of Graham. A jury could find the punches unjustified.

Clearly established. The court needed to look no further than Graham's holding that force is justified only when there is a need for force. That principle put a prudent officer on notice that gang tackling, without first attempting a less violent means of arrest, a relatively calm trespass suspect who had been cooperative in the past and was not actively resisting at the moment violated the Fourth Amendment; that punching him to free arms he was not using to resist was a violation; and that no reasonable officer would have believed hobble restraints on wrists and ankles, in addition to handcuffs, were necessary to control him and protect passersby. Gray, Nguyen, Ross and South were denied immunity on the tackle and punches; those four plus Kayano on the hobbles, under the integral participation rule, because Kayano's help in handcuffing was instrumental to the control that culminated in the hobbles and Gray ordered them. Montano (crowd control) and Roman (arrived afterward) were properly dismissed.

Municipal liability. Blankenhorn's failure to train evidence (Nguyen's evaluations, internal affairs interviews and prior complaints against him) focused exclusively on one officer. Under Alexander v. City and County of San Francisco, evidence of a failure to train a single officer is at most negligence, not the deliberate indifference City of Canton requires; a program wide inadequacy must be shown. Summary judgment for the city was affirmed.

Supervisory liability. Chief Romero approved Nguyen's evaluations despite three excessive force complaints that had each resulted in discipline (shaking an arrestee by the hair, ordering his dog to attack a child while off duty, pushing a woman in the breast), and the plaintiff's expert opined the discipline was inadequate and in one instance tantamount to none. Under Larez and Watkins, a rational fact finder could conclude Romero knowingly condoned and ratified conduct he should have known would cause constitutional injury. Summary judgment for Romero was reversed.

Malicious prosecution was reinstated against Nguyen, Ross and South based on evidence contradicting their reports. State law claims were reinstated except false arrest; California does not immunize officers who use unreasonable force, and the city may be vicariously liable.
notDecided:
Whether the officers in fact used excessive force. The court held only that genuine issues of material fact existed and that a rational jury could find the tackle, the punches and the hobbles unreasonable on Blankenhorn's version. The case was remanded.

Whether hobble restraints are unreasonable in general. The court said that in some situations the need to control a person who struggled during arrest might reasonably call for them.

Whether tackling or punching to make an arrest is excessive as such. The court said neither necessarily is; the question is need.

Whether the city's training program was deficient. The court held only that evidence about one officer cannot prove a municipal policy.

Whether Chief Romero is liable. A fact question remains, and the court noted that if no constitutional violation is proved on remand the supervisory claim would be moot.
inPractice:
Blankenhorn is the case to teach when the subject says no but has not done anything else. The officers had a lawful arrest. What they did not have, on the plaintiff's version, was a reason to go from a verbal refusal straight to a three officer tackle. The court's clearly established holding is simple enough to memorize: force is justified only when there is a need for force, and a prudent officer knows not to gang tackle a relatively calm, previously cooperative misdemeanant who is not actively resisting without first trying something less violent.

The hobble holding deserves attention because it turns on sequence. The officers argued the struggle justified the restraints. The court answered that if the officers' own sudden, unannounced, violent approach provoked the struggle, the arrestee had a limited right to resist reasonably, and restraints imposed because of that resistance could themselves be unreasonable. Restraint decisions are judged by what caused the need for them.

The punches holding is about the gap between technique and fact. A distraction strike to free trapped hands is a recognized technique; it is justified only if the hands are actually trapped. Reports that omitted the punches, which the video showed, cost the officer his credibility and cost the prosecution its case.

For agencies, the case splits two lines. Training liability against the city failed because the evidence was about one officer; a plaintiff must show program wide inadequacy. But the chief's personal exposure survived because he signed evaluations for an officer with three disciplined excessive force complaints and, on the expert's view, inadequate discipline. Supervisors who ratify a pattern can be reached even when the agency cannot.

Dr. Sowards teaches Blankenhorn in the arrest and control curriculum for the takedown decision and in the training liability line for the Monell and supervisor holdings.
trainIt:
Teach the step before the takedown. Build a scenario with a loud, profane, non-compliant misdemeanant who refuses to kneel. Require the student to announce the arrest, give the command, and attempt a controlled handcuffing or escort hold before any takedown, unless the student can articulate a threat or active resistance that makes those steps unsafe. The court's criticism was that the officers never tried to handcuff him before three of them tackled him.

Teach team takedowns as deliberate, not reflexive. Three officers moving at once without a signal or a plan reads to a court as a predetermined gang tackle. Train a lead officer, a verbal warning, and a coordinated control approach with defined roles.

Teach distraction strikes with their predicate. The technique is lawful when a prone subject is actually pinning his hands under his body. Students must be able to say what they saw and felt that showed the hands were trapped, and their report must say the same. Train the report to include every strike delivered.

Teach hobble and leg restraint decisions in context. The question the court asked was whether the officers' own conduct provoked the struggle that supposedly justified the restraints, and whether, once the subject was handcuffed and controlled, anything about him still required restraints on wrists and ankles. Require a stated reason for each added restraint, tied to current behavior.

For supervisors and training staff, teach both halves of the liability holding. Document training at the program level, because a single officer's gaps will not prove a municipal policy, and because a program wide gap will. And treat force complaints as a supervision event with a documented, proportionate response, because a signature on an evaluation that ignores them can be evidence of ratification.

Teach the posture: summary judgment reversed on the plaintiff's version of disputed facts, remand for trial, no finding of liability.
caution: The opinion was read from the Public.Resource.Org archive, which has no reporter pagination, so no pin cites are given. The facts are the plaintiff's version as the court was required to view them on summary judgment; the officers described a fighting stance, clenched fists, an announced gang affiliation and hands pinned under the body, and the video, obstructed and without audio, did not resolve those disputes. The court found triable issues, not liability. The probable cause holding drew a partial dissent from Judge Berzon.
dissent: Judge Berzon concurred in all of the majority opinion except its holding that the officers had probable cause to arrest for trespass. She read the statute requiring a refusal to leave upon being requested to require a contemporaneous request, found no evidence Blankenhorn intended to interfere with the mall's business, and would have held there was no probable cause under either trespass provision. She concurred in the result on the federal arrest claim because the intent based trespass provision was unclear enough to support qualified immunity, but would have allowed the state law false arrest claim to proceed. She joined the excessive force, municipal liability and supervisory liability holdings in full.

applications.title: Try the less violent means first
applications.body: The court held it was clearly established that gang tackling a relatively calm, previously cooperative misdemeanant who was not actively resisting, without first attempting a less violent means of arrest, violated the Fourth Amendment. A verbal refusal to kneel is not an invitation to tackle.

applications.title: Need is the heart of Graham
applications.body: The court needed to look no further than Graham's rule that force is only justified when there is a need for force. Every strike, tackle and restraint should be matched to a specific, articulable need at that moment.

applications.title: Provocation changes who is resisting
applications.body: An arrest attempted without warning, without trying to handcuff, by three officers at once, could reasonably be considered provocative, triggering the arrestee's limited right to reasonable resistance and making restraints imposed because of that resistance unreasonable.

applications.title: The technique needs its predicate
applications.body: Distraction punches to free trapped hands are justified only if the hands are trapped. The plaintiff denied it, the video did not show it, and the reports omitted the punches entirely. Report every strike and the fact that justified it.

applications.title: One officer's file is not a training policy
applications.body: Evidence about a single officer's training and complaints cannot show the program wide inadequacy that municipal liability requires. But a chief who approves evaluations despite repeated excessive force complaints may personally face a ratification claim.

applications.title: Posture
applications.body: Summary judgment was reversed on the excessive force, malicious prosecution, supervisory liability and most state law claims and affirmed on the arrest and municipal liability claims. The court found triable issues on the plaintiff's version of the facts, not liability.

quiz.q: What clearly established principle did the court rely on to deny qualified immunity for the gang tackle?
options: A prior Ninth Circuit case involving a shopping mall

Graham's holding that force is only justified when there is a need for force, which put a prudent officer on notice not to gang tackle a relatively calm, non-resisting trespass suspect without first attempting a less violent means of arrest
The city's use of force policy
The California Penal Code definition of trespass
quiz.teach: The court said it needed to look no further than Graham. The same principle gave notice that punching to free arms that were not being used to resist, and adding hobble restraints to a handcuffed and controlled arrestee, were violations.

quiz.q: Why did the court hold that a jury could find the hobble restraints unreasonable even though Blankenhorn struggled before being taken to the ground?
options: Because hobble restraints are always unconstitutional

Because the officers' unannounced, simultaneous, violent tackle could be found provocative, giving Blankenhorn a limited right to reasonable resistance, so restraints imposed because of that resistance could be unreasonable
Because the restraints were applied by a security guard
quiz.teach: The court accepted that hobbles can be reasonable to control someone who fought during arrest, but applied the rule from Span and Arpin that an officer who uses excessive force is not acting in good faith and that provocative conduct triggers a limited right to resist.

quiz.q: Why did the failure to train claim against the City of Orange fail while the claim against Chief Romero survived?
options: Because the city had a perfect training record

Because the plaintiff's training evidence concerned only Officer Nguyen, which cannot show a program wide deliberate indifference, while the chief personally approved Nguyen's evaluations despite three excessive force complaints that had drawn discipline, which a jury could see as ratification
Because cities cannot be sued under section 1983
quiz.teach: Under Alexander, a single officer's training gap is at most negligence, not the deliberate indifference City of Canton requires. Under Larez and Watkins, a supervisor who knowingly condones or ratifies a subordinate's conduct can be individually liable.
